newsitem.title: GUAM: Jumbo jet barely recognisable after Guam crash.
newsitem.headline: Jumbo jet barely recognisable after Guam crash.

text.p: The Boeing 747 was barely recognisable on Wednesday night, wreckage strewn across the hillside of this Pacific island still smouldering more than 16 hours after the plane slammed into the ground and burst into flames.
Only the tail section, with the clearly visible Korean Air Lines logo, was relatively intact.
The rest of the fuselage had broken into more than six major hunks of metal. The first-class section came to rest more than 75 feet (25 metres) away from the rest of the plane.

The search for survivors among the 254 people aboard the aircraft was made more grim by the presence of grieving relatives who were allowed near the site of the crash, mingling with reporters and onlookers.
Debris from the $165 million plane that might someday prove critical to determining the cause of the tragedy littered the side of the road on the way to the site.
Clothing from burst suitcases and bottles from the plane's pantry were spread across a wide area, mixed with leftover bandages from the frenzied rescue attempt.
The scrub brush and high grass that covered the hill was blackened in spots.
The first rescuers who arrived at the scene said the high grass turned the scene into a nightmare since nothing could be seen in the darkness. They were guided by the screams of injured passengers.
Among the first at the scene was the island's governor, Carl Gutierrez, who raced through the brush with only a flashlight. He is credited with rescuing some of the passengers.

"The fire was not so big, so we had to follow the sounds. It was eerie and as we got closer I heard all the screams coming from the dark spots ... We had to follow the sounds," he said in a conference call with reporters.
Within hours, hundreds of U.S. military personnel in khaki uniforms were combing the area, looking for passengers who may have been tossed far away to relative safety by the force of the crash.

But by Wednesday evening, the rescuers had all but given up hope of finding more people alive. Admiral Martin Janczak announced that while the search for survivors could continue with specially-trained tracking dogs, he saw no reason to go on.
That left only 30 survivors from the 231 passengers and 23 crew on board.
As night fell, the military cleared away onlookers from the area and continued its work -- not in the hopes of finding anyone alive but to search for more bodies.
